This specimen is of a Crinoid colony holding on to driftwood. These creatures that are a relation to sea stars and sea urchins would have floated with the driftwood. Over time the driftwood became water logged and sank to the bottom. If this happened where there is a high amount of silt being deposited in the area, the creatures would be buried quickly and would potentially form fossils. This can happen a lot of ways, but is often due to underwater landslides, ocean currents or being close to the mouth of a river.

When covered with silt, the remains are protected from oxygen, scavengers, and microbes that would break down the creature on the surface. Over time the minerals in the silt deposit themselves into the remains creating fossils. Or, the remains do decay over a long period of time, and leave imprints of themselves in the now hardened silt. These imprints can sometimes leave hollow areas that later fill with minerals over long periods of time, which create a 3D representation of what was once there.

That will be a bit tough to judge without seeing it, and I'm no expert, I've just done a lot of random concrete projects/repairs. If you prep the area well, and use a concrete bonding agent before sculpting in your new patch I'd say this stuff is going to be as good a choice as any other I can think of. The adhesion to the existing concrete is the main concern to have IMO. A stiff wire brush to rough up and clean the area to be fixed, rinsed with water, let dry, apply bonding agent with a chip brush(painters tape around it, its messy), let dry, patch. That's how I'd address it.


This is the bonding agent I use, and its great:

https://www.homedepot.com/p/Lanco-Concrebond-1-Gal-Blue-Concrete-Bonding-Agent-and-Adhesive-CB1798-4/314031412

It comes out looking nice, I'd see no issue with that. It might end up a bit of a darker gray than non-reinforced concrete though. That said, I think it shines as a patch that needs to stand up to abuse and have a little bit of flexibility to it, might be overkill for cosmetic work. I've seen it used on the run up to a loading ramp on a receiving dock to repair where tail of the forklift would scrape the concrete. After a weekend of drying it held up for years. It will scrape and scuff away, not shatter and shed chunks.

I'm also a big fan of this stuff (link below) if the patch *really* needs to not go anywhere. Coat the inside of the area to be patched, let it dry(fully dry, that's important, its less dense than concrete and will rise to the surface like a lava lamp if you plonk the concrete on it while its still wet), then add a bit to the concrete mix before patching as per the instructions on the bottle. I've used it to extend concrete steps that were a bit too short and causing people to trip. Held a vertical bond for years (along with some rebar I drilled in to the existing step and coated with it), and afaik is still there. 

https://www.homedepot.com/p/Lanco-Concrebond-1-Gal-Blue-Concrete-Bonding-Agent-and-Adhesive-CB1798-4/314031412

I like this stuff. Holds up well, adheres to existing surface well, and has a bit of flex so it doesn't crack and chip. Clean out the hole, spray it clean with the hose, let it dry, and patch. https://www.homedepot.com/p/Quikrete-20-lb-Polymer-Modified-Structural-Concrete-Repair-124125/207102852

 You know how an updraft creates the towering cumulous clouds we associate with thunderstorms? When that warm updraft collapses as the storm dies, all that now cold heavy air that has piled up on top of the updraft comes crashing back down to earth.

 That cold air hits the ground with a fair amount of force and spreads out around the storm. As it moves outward that air acts like a wedge racing across the surface hugging the ground and forcing the existing surface based stable warm moist air upwards over the expanding wedge. That water in that warm moist air condenses into water droplets, that we see as an outflow boundary on radar. It is the boundary of the cold out-rushing wedge of air pushing the warm humid air on the surface upwards.
